newsitem.title: UK: B.A.T plays down tobacco insurance cover.
newsitem.headline: B.A.T plays down tobacco insurance cover.

text.p: B.A.T Industries Plc chairman Lord Cairns on Friday played down suggestions that the tobacco giant may rely on insurance cover to offset future tobacco-related claims against the company.

Speaking at the annual meeting, Cairns said B.A.T's confidence that outstanding tobacco litigation would not have a material impact on the financial condition of the group was not reliant on insurance cover and that the group remained "confident of winning cases."

The tobacco industry is facing thousands of individual claims from sufferers of smoking-related diseases in the U.S. as well as being sued by more than 20 states to cover the costs of treating smokers.

The tobacco industry is reportedly in talks with state officials over a possible settlement of lawsuits, including a proposed $300 billion to be paid by the industry into a fund for smoking related injuries over the next 25 years.

Asked by a shareholder about the extent of exclusions in general insurance policy documents taken out by B.A.T for tobacco-related claims, Cairns replied that the whole issue of product liability was "highly complicated" involving "many insurers over many years with different policy wording and exclusion notes."
Cairns, however, said it was not in the long term interest of shareholders to make any further public comment on the issue at this stage.

Schroders insurance analyst Paul Hodges suggested in a recent report that loosely worded general liability insurance policies through the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s could open the way for tobacco related liability claims against insurance companies.
The bottom line, argues Hodges, is that the exclusionary language in the insurance policies is nowhere near tight enough and unlikely to be a significant bar to coverage.
Last month, the Louisiana attorney-general named more than 100 insurance companies as co-defendants in its action against tobacco companies.
Tobacco firms have refused to be drawn on the prospect of suing insurers while the insurance companies have been quick to dismiss the chances of large-scale claims against them.
But, says Hodges, it is in neither group's interests to talk about it and action against the insurers would involve three costs to tobacco firms.
Firstly, it would open up a litigation battle on a second front.
Secondly, the insurer would become legally entitled to take control of the tobacco manufacturers defence in cases pending against them.
Thirdly, under U.S. powers of discovery, the insurers would be afforded almost unlimited access to internal documents, some of which may be embarrassing and likely to generate negative publicity.
"Tobacco manufacturers are not going to undertake such actions until the benefits exceed those costs and they're under no pressure to make an early decision on it," said Hodges.

-- Simon Cowell, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7721 Going back to 1930s1940s, 1950s, 1960s - devotes lot of time looking at poliucy exclusions used by insurance cos to cover themselves in that period. Louisiana attorney general - attornieys taken view policy exclusions weka up to 1970 and policies issued as late as last year may not exclude coverage for the type of claim being poursued by the attorney general. wisconsin and new hampshire also have direct action statutes.
